Regardless of whether or not she made propaganda films for the Nazis, she remained close with Hitler, Goebbels and the Nazi intellectual class throughout the war as far as I know. She conveniently claims that she didn't know about the Holocaust, but a lot of Nazis and people involved in the Nazi government said that. Her film Tiefland used Romani slave labor from a nearby concentration camp as extras, and then those extras were later sent to Auschwitz.

Although she wasn't found formally guilty she was absolutely complicit in the Nazi's crimes and her propaganda films carry all the hallmarks of Nazi propaganda. Hitler was a racist, anti-semitic, fascist white supremacist well before the Nazis started exterminating Jews and other groups they deemed undesirable en masse. He was very clear as far back as Mein Kampf (1925) and before that he wanted a white German ethnostate and the eradication of German Jews. Someone as well read and educated as Riefenstahl would have known this, Hitler was completely open about his genocidal goals and desire for a pan-European fascist dictatorship.

>Obsession with the strong, physical form is a classic hallmark of fascism.

This is a non-starter of an argument but unfortunately, it always gets brought up when people start going on about fascist aesthetics (which just like the word fascist itself, has had its meaning totally diluted to the point of meaninglessness).

Like yes, you could say that fascism values strength, but it's a bit like arguing that fascists breathe oxygen. Or that "violent criminal XYZ is found to have a copy of Grand Theft Auto". The correlation is so broad that it invalidates any actual point.

I've read Riefenstahl's memoir (which I do recommend, because I found the pre-war, Weimar era Bergfilme filmmaking stories to be quite harrowing and fascinating) and she claims ignorance with a little of "I didn't agree/didn't want to know/did it because I was pressured by Goebbels." I don't believe that she could have possibly been as in the dark as she claims, but I can see how there was no doubt an enormous amount of pressure on her coming from the Third Reich combined with the uniqueness of her position as a woman filmmaker.

Whether or not you believe Riefenstahl was clued in on how exactly serious Hitler was about his beliefs is a whole can of worms that extends to millions of other people living in Germany. Hindsight is 20/20 and it's well-documented how many Germans supported Hitler because they were desperate. I am not saying that that absolves responsibility, but very few people could have imagined or foreseen the Holocaust, and those that could probably didn't want to. It's a sad story and one that is much bigger than Leni Riefenstahl. 

The facts of Riefenstahl's life don't lead to the conclusion that she was on the same ideological plane as the Nazis. After the war, she spent a considerable amount of time in Africa creating photographic books of the Nuba people. She learned their culture and lived with them for extended periods of time, and she did it solo as a 60-something-year-old woman.  

I don't understand where you're going with your point about Jesse Owens, can you clarify? It sounds like you're saying that by including Jesse Owens, Riefenstahl was trying to show the strength of Aryan men which... doesn't make any sense..

Riefenstahl was both complicit to the Nazi's and an incredible filmmaker. For some reason people cant seem to recognize those two aspects of her together. Her films are seminal works in filmmaking language. People who dismiss her work are usually driven by their feelings towards what those films represented vs what they achieved.

Take *Triumph of the Will* and lets compare it to Griffith's *Birth of a Nation.* Griffith is generally seen is a similar light to Riefenstahl. He was an amazing filmmaker but the racism in *Birth of a Nation* is indisputable. Now, whether or not you view Griffith as a racist often depends on whether or not you think is follow-up *Intolerance* was a valid rebuke to his critics. 

I think his biographer Richard Schickel put it best when he wrote regarding the matter: “that high artistic vision does not necessarily correlate with a similarly elevated social vision.”

Does the artist represent the art and vice versa? In Griffith's case, he'd argue that the art did not represent him. In Riefenstahl's case, one would argue that maybe the artist did not represent the art. 

Riefenstahl had serious Nazi ties. She was often rubbing shoulders with Hitler, Goebbels and the rest of the elite. Was she there because she shared their values? Maybe not. Did she exploit their support to make the films she wanted? Absolutely. However, like Griffith (who's reputation is not disputed despite his controversy), she was a pioneer in her art. She deserves all the praise and recognition. I believe what she did is underappreciated and her reputation is overshadowed by the propaganda in her films. She certainly deserves all the scrutiny and criticism directed at her but you cannot ignore her talent.

Fascist aesthetics are one of the most widely written about subjects in the art world and I would recommend you read up on that before posting more (hopefully) accidental Nazi apologia like you've done here.

Reading a Nazi propagandist defend herself is not something I feel like I need to spend my time doing. There are many accounts of the Weimar film industry that weren't written by Nazi propagandists.

>very few people could have imagined or foreseen the Holocaust, and those that could probably didn't want to. It's a sad story and one that is much bigger than Leni Riefenstahl.

It's absolutely not a "sad story" for someone as plugged into the Nazi intelligentsia and propaganda machine as Riefenstahl. Goebbels was a genocidal maniac and made no secret of that, especially into the 40s. You can hem and haw about whether or not Riefenstahl was a true believer, but Goebbels was. This is just textbook Holocaust denial to be perfectly honest. Just constantly shifting the goalposts to absolve the German people of any wrongdoing until you get to a point where you're now denying that one of the Nazi's most popular and influential propagandists was just an unfortunate, misled soul.

>The facts of Riefenstahl's life don't lead to the conclusion that she was on the same ideological plane as the Nazis. After the war, she spent a considerable amount of time in Africa creating photographic books of the Nuba people. She learned their culture and lived with them for extended periods of time, and she did it solo as a 60-something-year-old woman.

You understand that this in no way absolves her of her work with the Nazis, no? You shouldn't get to make propaganda films for a genocidal fascist and then live out the rest of your life peacefully. She was found not guilty by virtue of having no direct role in planning or carrying out the Holocaust but just because a court found her not guilty doesn't mean that we can't judge her correctly.
What country won the most medals at the 1936 olympics

What exactly are you trying to say here? Germany won the most medals so they were correct about aryan men being superior? Is that *really* something you think is 1) correct to begin with and 2) worth pointing out? Has this sub really declined to the point where people are posting shit like "well the Nazis DID have a point about the physical superiority of Aryan men".

Other people have written better comments, so my bottom line is that yes, she does have a significant amount of technical innovations worth mearning from in terms of visual metaphor, imagery and like filmic techniques countless people have borrowed, and she made the single most well-known nazi propoganda. This isn’t an either/or situation, it’s easy to condemn her and recognize she had some novel ideas most filmmakers use at some time or another, or that aside from the content, these films are trchnically worth learning from.

Still, it’s a complicated issue saying something like that, as it was a direct intention of the Nazis to be spoken of in term of how hyper competent they were and to perpetuate the idea that idea of superiority and have sympathizers who could approach them on these multiple fronts. I think it’s very easy to condemn the machine but narcek at how the gears interlock, but when it comes to Reifenstahl herself, the bottom line is that she actively profited from making Nazi propaganda, and that is worth condemning regardless of extenuating factors.

Just wanted to chime in here in agreement/support of u/Professional_Dot9888. I received my Ph.D. in Modern European History and taught the rise of fascism, the Nazi era, and the Holocaust multiple times.

As Dot said, an obsession with strength and the physical form was a defining feature of all fascist movements. Sure, you can claim that in some kind of vague, ambient sense many societies have been interested in promoting physical strength, but very few make it critical to their aesthetic and political program. To take a contemporary example, the British Empire didn't promote an image of the muscular Englishman as the successor of Greek martial culture. Ditto the French.

In the same way, fascist societies were also obsessed with politicizing women's bodies and the home front more broadly. So while men were supposed to be muscular and athletic, women were supposed to be fertile and nurturing. This represents a classic fascist trait, namely, the extension of the state into every aspect of society until the two are essentially coextensive. Remember, in the case of Nazi Germany we're talking about a society that murdered over 200,000 of its own citizens as part of the T4 program to rid Germany society of those it deemed mentally and physically inferior, i.e. the disabled, the sick, the infirmed, etc. This is the literal culmination of the fascist impulse to physical strength, and it's something in which Riefenstahl is inextricably implicated.

I'll also add that while "fascism" is a debated term, no serious scholars dispute that it's an apt description of Mussolini's Italy, Hitler's Germany (and Austria), or Franco's Spain. I highly recommend you read a classic in the field like Robert Paxton's *The Anatomy of Fascism* to better understand the beliefs, iconography, organizing principles, and prejudices of fascist society.

>Can we really blame her for using what was in front of her, when this was before the horrors of the Holocaust really took place and before WWII started?

Other people have written fuller comments but western critical consensus is that yes highly innovative filmmaker who was absolutely both complicit and an active participant in the rise of fascism in 1930s Europe leading to the horrors of WWII and various genocides. The specific questions of what she knew when are basically closed due to lack of reliable contemporaneous evidence. There's no need to make a simplistic Riefenstahl good vs Riefenshtahl bad argument like you seem to be doing.

>You shouldn't get to make propaganda films for a genocidal fascist and then live out the rest of your life peacefully.

Except the propaganda films that she worked on were made many years before the true genocide of the Holocaust. There's nothing in them that advocates for the horrors of what the Nazis would later do. Have you even watched her films?

It's not Holocaust denial to say that the average German in 1934 could not predict what would happen by 1944. Stop arguing in bad faith; obviously, all the German people were complicit on some level. Condemning them is important, but even more important is that we learn how these things happen slowly and silently because as long as these complicit acts remain at an intellectual and moral distance, we will be doomed to eventually repeat them. Most of us would probably be guilty of the same level of complicity if the choice was between death and ignorance.

Riefenstahl's work is stylistically gorgeous but ideologically hollow. There's nothing about the artistry of *Triumph of the Will* or *Olympia* that seems to endorse the Nazi's evil ideology beyond it simply makes the subjects look nice - which you could hypothetically apply to anything, and that's largely why her work is so influential. Again, I don't believe her claims to total ignorance, but upon analyzing her work, it would be reaching to say she was a believer.

Except that seems to be what's happening with the "western critical consensus" being less interested in the quality of her work and more with its ideological ties. 

Which I think is quite missing the point since if you look at her work, regardless of her beliefs IRL, it's quite ideologically shallow. Stylistically and technically, she was extravagant, even unmatched - but it seems clear that she didn't have a lot to say.

This isn't a direct response to OP but just a general PSA for anyone in doubt as to Riefenstahl's complicity in Nazi crimes. Read about the crusading German journalist Nina Gladitz who spent her life negating the filmmaker's attempts to obfuscate her own exploitation of forced labour and clear knowledge of concentration and death camps.

Gladitz' journalism is lesser known outside of Germany but the UK newspaper The Guardian did an excellent job in putting together an extended obituary and overview of her life's work in English. You can check it out [here](https://www.theguardian.com/news/2021/dec/09/burying-leni-riefenstahl-nina-gladitz-lifelong-crusade-hitler-film-maker). Thanks to Gladitz' relentless efforts we now know definitively that Riefenstahl's involvement wasn't merely "white collar".

As a forum for discussing film, I can’t let the opportunity pass to recommend The Wonderful Horrible Life of Leni Riefenstahl by Ray Muller. It was made with her full cooperation but it invariably runs into problems as her denials are repeatedly shown to be incomplete or insincere.

>It's not Holocaust denial to say that the average German in 1934 could not predict what would happen by 1944.

So it's ok to vote for antisemitic fascists since we can't predict what they will do later ? What is wrong with you ?

Watch the films. That's it.

I see that my earlier comment was judged too brief and I can understand why the right answer is problematical from a certain point of view.

I should go into a long dissertation as to why your opinion of Riefenstahl's films should be formed by the films themselves but I have too much respect for the intelligence of members of this forum to waste your time on such a long & unnecessary exercise when what I want to say, on point, does not require anything like that.

Condemning them is important, but even more important is that we learn how these things happen slowly and silently because as long as these complicit acts remain at an intellectual and moral distance, we will be doomed to eventually repeat them.

Part of engaging with these difficult questions is recognizing when someone like Riefenstahl is the one operating in bad faith. Taking everything at face value and trusting the words of a friend to Hitler and Goebbels seems like an interesting place to start in trying to understand how the Holocaust happened.

I just want to point out that anti-Jewish discrimination by the Nazi party started as early as 1933 and the Nuremberg laws (actually enshrining the discrimination in law) were implemented in 1935, all well before a single Jew was killed by the German state as part of the Holocaust.

Did I say that? No, I didn’t. I said that the average German who voted for Hitler never would have if they could clearly see what would eventually happen, to both themselves and the 12 million innocents murdered. Stop with this false equivalence BS.

You don't have to defend Riefenstahl's reputation: it is cemented, her impact upon film culture, and documentary specifically, is well-documented and important.

If you feel you must defend her against accusations of being in cahoots with Nazi's, regardless of how much she knew or whatever, that says more about you than it does about her. A great artist can be a terrible person; we all should know this by now.

One of my favorite writers is Ezra Pound. His work has been profoundly impactful upon my work, but I feel no need nor impetus to defend his fascist beliefs and actions. It does not change the work for me, but it may for other people, and that's okay because actions and beliefs should have consequences.

>the infamous Tiefland, which while not good, was certainly not a propaganda movie.

The film about the noble teutonic blond guy rescuing our heroine from a dark-complexioned villain obsessed with wealth? The film that used [concentration camp inmates as unpaid extras](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2002/aug/18/artsandhumanities.germany)?

You're acculturated... 1931 the NSDAP published a poster, the famous "500 000 unemployed 400 000 jews, the solution is here". Read at least some pages of Hitler's "Mein Kampf"... and then tell me *Muuuh, average people couldn't predict...* You don't need to predict. The early beginning should alert you. End of the story.

I'm not even talking about your pitiful attempt to rehabilitate the work of Riefensthal, that's not the point anymore. You're clearly trying to disculpate people who voted for the far right. Like it's ok to vote for Putine, or Hamas, Or Rassemblement National or Erdogan or Netanyahou... Read some history, try to figure out something about politics, then we would talk about cinematography.

For me, she was an amazing Filmmaker and her achievement of being a professional woman in Nazi Germany is noteworthy. That said, she also made work that ultimately supported the regime and she shouldn't get a free pass. She was an artist and a problematic individual, basically complicated.

Yeah, I do think that that doc is very interesting because you can see how she's in denial of something - it's just never clear what exactly she knew or signed off on. The moral ambiguity, rationalizations, and insecurities are on full display.

Yeah, I do think that that doc is very interesting because you can see how she's in denial of something - it's just never clear what exactly she knew or signed off on. The moral ambiguity, rationalizations, and insecurities are on full display.

Gladitz' "journalism" is (as The Guardian article that you linked points out) extremely questionable because of how obviously vindictive she was. Making it her personal mission to tear down Riefenstahl's professional reputation *for nearly forty years* and draw attention to herself in the process was never a good look, and it makes her claims difficult to believe. Critics said as much and the legal record has never shifted.

I don't believe Riefenstahl was innocent of wrongdoing by any means, but Nina Gladitz was obviously paranoid and delusional if you actually read her writing. I mean Christ, she got rejected by over 30 publishers, and she claimed that it was because the mainstream media wouldn't dare tarnish the reputation of a Nazi sympathizer.

I think the problem is that there seems to be a growing acceptance, academically, of the idea that we *should not* separate art from artist. I was in film school a few years ago and the professor made learning about Riefenstal completely optional because they didn't want any students to feel uncomfortable or challenged.

To me, that is a severe regression and fundamentally anti-intellectual. Frankly, I think the discussion about how guilty she was of being in with Hitler is a discussion worth having, because: 

A.) We don't have a reliable source outside of the legal record.

B.) Her being a woman in her position could have made it harder for her to say no and/or harder for her to want to say no given the rarity of her opportunity. Many second wave feminists admired her as a pioneering woman in film, and honestly, I think that, to a certain understandable degree, that's valid.

C.) Her propaganda films were made long before the Nazis had written themselves into the darkest chapters of modern history books. Artists being swept up in political movements, especially in the age of mass media, is commonplace and to me Riefenstahl's tale is a cautionary one about the cost of opportunity, complicit ignorance, and artistic freedom that bears relevance to today's landscape for all artists.

She was a first class propagandist who was good at her job and well rewarded for it. Life for her was sweet in those Nazi years.   Leni delivered the goods to build the Nazi myths her paymasters needed to keep the war machine running full blast.  

Her Nazi propaganda directly encouraged untold thousands of German youths - thrilled by her films - to march to their deaths, and much worse.  

You can separate the artist from their work, but you can’t separate the work from the artist.

And *if* she was such a wonderful artist, why didn’t she pack her bags and move to California?

>And if she was such a wonderful artist, why didn’t she pack her bags and move to California?

Her two major propaganda films (and her silent films before in the Weimar era) were internationally celebrated; no reasonable person can deny that she was a talented artist. She actually met with Walt Disney and a few other major American execs, but it was a year after *Olympia,* and by then the Nazis' antisemitism was becoming very loud and active. She was effectively blacklisted because of this. And very soon after that, the war started. For her pre-war work, Hitler gave her a huge budget to make *Tiefland*, a film that she likely could have never made anywhere else. At the very least she sold her soul.

You are making my point for me.  Of course she was talented, and she  channeled that talent into churning out Nazi mythmaking propaganda.“

After all these Hollywood meetings, the guy who really shares her vision and writes the biggest check is Hitler.  What does that tell you?

Btw, I very much disagree with you re: LR, but your post is thoughtful and articulate.  I think this is an interesting topic for discussion.  How do you separate the art from the artist?  In LR’s case, she is so closely aligned with, and built her career around, Nazi myth making and propaganda, I don’t think you can separate the two.

Yeah, you're talking out of your ass. The Holocaust didn't start with the war. The first Nazi concentration camp was built in 1933. Dachau, one of the most notorious camps, was also opened in 1933. 
The Nürnberger Rassengesetze were passed in 1935.
Hitlers positions were well known and well documented, Mein Kampf had been released in 1925.
The SS also existed since 1925 and along with the SA it attacked and murdered Jews, Communists and Social Democrats. They were also instrumental in ensuring the passing of the Ermächtigungsgesetz in 1933, that granted Hitler absolute authority, by intimidating and threatening all opposition. There were Pogroms and boycotts of Jewish shops, laws that banned Jews from certain and then most professions before they were as widely deported. Even if they didn't know the whole extent of the Nazis crimes, most Germans knew what was going on. They knew.
And Riefenstahl was complicit, she was a part of what made it work. 
Stop trying to rehabilitate Nazis, they tried the same with Speer, who claimed to have had no idea of what was going on. People like you, who are obviously ignorant of historical events are incredibly dangerous.

yeah by the time Reifenstahl made her propaganda films the government had merely imprisoned its political opponents in concentration camps; mandated the forcible sterilization of anybody with genetic diseases such as mental illness, epilepsy, blindness, and being black; stripped Jews of German citizenship and the right to vote; barred Jews from working in medicine, law, politics, civil service, journalism, agriculture, and film-making; repeatedly gave speeches about Jews being the eternal enemy of the Aryan race; and other things that weren't really a big deal. Can we blame her?

I am getting my PhD. in Creative Writing and Screen Studies, so I have been taking a lot of graduate film classes, took a film exam, etc. And I can tell you that your anecdotal evidence does not reflect my experience whatsoever. I watched Reifenstal and several other "problematic" filmmakers and had discussions of them.

You keep accusing everyone who disagrees with you of being anti-intellectual because I guess if someone disagrees with you, they must not be an intellectual.

But ignoring that, the idea that someone should separate the art from the artist is an argument, not a fact of nature. It is a fairly new argument, and it has had several iterations. It is not necessarily anti-intellectual to not separate the art from the artist because that is just one argument, among many, for how we should approach art.

I just don't feel the need to defend a Nazi. She made her choices, and she had her impacts, as did myriad other filmmakers who were not Nazis.
